levels.title: High-Alert Brand Recognition
levels.description: Differentiate deceptive brand names that look and sound nearly identical.
levels.learningObjective: Distinguish between deceptive brand names like Actonel and Actos.

activities.learningObjective: Distinguish look-alike and sound-alike brand names from verified ISMP pairs.

questions.prompt: Which medication name is the documented Look-Alike / Sound-Alike counterpart that is dangerously confused with Actonel?
questions.explanation: Actonel and Actos look and sound remarkably similar. Distinguishing their spellings prevents serious brand name mix-ups.

questions.prompt: Which vaccine product name is a documented look-alike and sound-alike counterpart to Adacel (Tdap)?
questions.explanation: Adacel (Tdap) and Daptacel (DTaP) have nearly identical name components and are frequently confused.

levels.title: Interactive Pair Matching
levels.description: Rapidly connect look-alike and sound-alike counterparts through tactile retrieval matching.
levels.learningObjective: Reinforce cognitive associations between confusable pairs under active retrieval conditions.

activities.learningObjective: Match each medication with its documented confusable counterpart.

questions.prompt: Match each medication with its documented confusable counterpart:
questions.explanation: Activase and TNKase are confusable thrombolytic names. Actonel and Actos look and sound similar. Adacel and Daptacel are confusable vaccines. Ado-trastuzumab and trastuzumab differ by the critical 'ado-' prefix.

levels.title: Situational Brand & Conjugate Recognition
levels.description: Discriminate complex prefix additions and sound-alike brand names in dispensing scenarios.
levels.learningObjective: Recognize target medication names in realistic pharmacy verification scenarios.

activities.learningObjective: Recognize the correct medication name in realistic dispensing review scenarios.

questions.scenario: A hospital oncology order requests conventional trastuzumab. When reviewing inventory, the automated dispensing cabinet also stocks the antibody-drug conjugate ado-trastuzumab emtansine.
questions.prompt: Which product name matches the requested order for conventional trastuzumab?
questions.explanation: Trastuzumab and ado-trastuzumab emtansine are distinct formulations. Verifying the 'ado-' prefix prevents fatal dosing confusion.

questions.scenario: A patient drops off a written prescription order for Advair. The pharmacy shelf also contains bottles of Advicor.
questions.prompt: Which medication product matches the prescription order for Advair?
questions.explanation: Advair and Advicor sound and look similar. Verifying the suffix ensures the intended medication is selected.

levels.title: Unit 3 Mastery
levels.description: Comprehensive review and unassisted Tall Man lettering mastery for Unit 3.
levels.learningObjective: Demonstrate complete unit mastery of brand/conjugate discrimination and unassisted Tall Man lettering without prompts or scaffolding.

activities.learningObjective: Review deceptive look-alike brand pairings under mastery evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which medication is the high-alert thrombolytic counterpart confusable with Activase?
questions.explanation: Activase (alteplase) and TNKase (tenecteplase) are easily confused thrombolytic agents with different dosing guidelines.

activities.learningObjective: Independently construct the exact Tall Man lettering for acetazolamide without scaffolding.

questions.prompt: UNIT MASTERY CAPSTONE TASK: Type the complete drug name using correct Tall Man lettering (capitalizing the specific distinguishing letters):
questions.explanation: acetaZOLAMIDE capitalizes ZOLAMIDE to differentiate this carbonic anhydrase inhibitor from acetoHEXAMIDE and acetaminophen.
